items.title: SWOT analysis is often misused as a sorting exercise
items.claim: SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) emerged from Albert Humphrey's work at Stanford in the 1960s-70s. What's the standard critique?

options.text: It is a complete strategic plan
SWOT identifies factors but provides no method to translate them into strategy; without TOWS-style cross-pairing (S-O, S-T, W-O, W-T), it's just four bullet-point lists
It can only be used for new ventures

items.reveal:
Heinz Weihrich's 1982 TOWS matrix paired Strengths with Opportunities (offensive strategies), Strengths with Threats (defensive), Weaknesses with Opportunities (improvement), and Weaknesses with Threats (mitigation).

The core SWOT critique is that without this step, the framework lists factors without forcing a strategic choice. Most student SWOTs stop at the list stage — which is descriptive, not strategic.
items.why: SWOT looks like analysis but often delivers sorting. The strategic value is in the combinations across quadrants.

items.title: Herzberg's hygiene factors don't motivate
items.claim: Frederick Herzberg's 1959 'Motivation to Work' surveyed 200 engineers and accountants. What did he conclude about pay?

options.text: Pay is a 'hygiene factor' — low pay causes dissatisfaction but high pay does not produce sustained motivation. Motivators are achievement, recognition and the work itself
Pay had no effect either way
Only senior staff are motivated by pay

items.reveal:
Herzberg's two-factor theory splits job factors into hygiene (pay, conditions, supervision, policies) — whose absence causes dissatisfaction — and motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) — which actively drive engagement.

Methodological critics note Herzberg used the 'critical incident' interview technique, in which people tend to attribute good experiences to themselves and bad ones to external factors. Replications using other methods get less crisp results.
items.why: Pay rises buy off dissatisfaction, not loyalty or effort. Most modern HR practice combines compensation (hygiene) with job design (motivators) — a direct legacy of Herzberg.

items.title: Maximising capacity utilisation isn't always optimal
items.claim: A factory runs at 95% capacity utilisation. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: This is always the optimal level
Running close to maximum capacity leaves no slack for demand surges, breakdowns or staff absence and tends to raise unit costs through overtime and quality problems
Capacity utilisation has no link to unit cost
Unit costs fall continuously with utilisation

items.reveal:
Hospitals running at >90% bed occupancy have measurably worse patient outcomes (NHS England analyses through the 2010s). Airlines running above 85% load factor face cascading delay risk. Manufacturing plants above 90% have higher defect rates and overtime costs.

Operations researchers use Kingman's formula: waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%. The textbook assumption that high utilisation is good ignores queueing dynamics.
items.why: Headline utilisation numbers hide trade-offs. The optimal level depends on demand variability, not just on fixed-cost recovery.
